AI Factory Case Studies · Part 9 · Sovereign AI factories

Compute as Sovereignty: Stargate UAE, Humain and the Race for National AI Factories

Governments now treat AI compute the way they once treated ports, refineries and power grids. The UAE is building a 1 GW cluster with OpenAI; Saudi Arabia's Humain is buying NVIDIA systems by the tens of thousands; the EU is choosing up to seven AI gigafactories; Norway is turning hydropower into GPU capacity; India subsidises GPUs for its startups. This case study compares what was announced with what has been delivered, and shows how much each project still depends on US chips, US labs and US export licences.

The reported redesign of the UAE campus comes from a Reuters exclusive we could only read through secondary reports. Security and geopolitical details change quickly. 3. The bet: compute as national infrastructure

Every earlier case study was built by a company to make money from AI. Sovereign projects add other goals: keeping sensitive data inside national borders, building a domestic AI industry, attracting foreign labs and investment, and gaining leverage in negotiations with the US. Governments and state-backed funds bring what companies find hardest to get: land, energy, permits and patient capital. What they mostly cannot bring is the chips or the frontier models, which still come from the US.

💡 Stargate, exportedStargate UAE and Stargate Norway reuse the Abilene model from Part 2: a local partner builds and owns the site, US companies supply chips, cloud and models, and OpenAI is the anchor customer. The difference is that a government is part of the deal, and an export licence is part of the risk.

4. Announced vs delivered

The headline and the first real tranche

Megawatts announced as the eventual goal against the first concrete, dated tranche, on a log scale. Hatched bars are not yet confirmed as running.

Sovereign projects are announced at the scale of national ambition and delivered at the scale of what chips, power and partners allow. Humain's May 2025 framing of up to 500 MW became an 84 MW, two-phase NVIDIA deal in October 2026. Stargate UAE's first 200 MW, due in Q3 2026, had not been documented as running by mid-October and is now pointed at Q4. Stargate Norway changed customer when OpenAI did not close its offtake and Microsoft took the capacity.

5. The dependency

Who each project depends on

Tap a project to highlight its links to chip suppliers, lab or cloud partners and the licences it needs. Simplified.

Every project in this article runs on NVIDIA chips, and the largest ones depend on US labs and clouds as anchor customers. Gulf deals involving advanced US chips have required US export licences and, as reported, security commitments about who can access the hardware and how it is protected ⚠️. Europe's gigafactories aim to give European researchers and companies their own capacity, but will still buy mostly US accelerators. India's compute portal rents GPUs from private providers under a government subsidy, and Business Standard reported in October 2026 that chip supply is now the main bottleneck.

6. Energy as a national advantage

Gulf: gas and sunCheap natural gas and large solar resources, plus state control of land and grids, let the UAE and Saudi Arabia promise gigawatts quickly. Heat makes cooling harder.
Norway: hydropowerNarvik offers cheap, clean hydropower and a cold climate. Stargate Norway was announced at 230 MW with room for another 290 MW, aiming for 100,000 GPUs.
EU and India: grid limitsEurope's gigafactories must find sites with enough grid capacity, one reason 18 member states and 76 consortia are competing for at most seven. India's compute is spread across private data centers.

7. Security

Sovereign AI factories in the Gulf now face a risk none of the US case studies did. Iranian drones struck AWS facilities in the UAE and Bahrain on 1 March 2026, according to DCD, Asia Society and others, and Iran's Revolutionary Guard named the Stargate campus in Abu Dhabi as a potential target. Reuters later reported, in an exclusive we could read only through secondary coverage ⚠️, that the UAE was revising the 5 GW campus into several smaller, hardened sites, with air defences and some underground construction under consideration, while keeping the first phase of Stargate UAE broadly on track with added protection. No official UAE announcement of the redesign had been made as of this writing.

⚖️ A new kind of riskEarlier case studies worried about permits, debt and water. In the Gulf, AI factories are now treated as potential military targets, and their design is changing as a result: spread out, defended, partly underground. That raises costs and may slow delivery.

8. Europe's gigafactories

The EU call, explained

EuroHPC's call for AI gigafactories, opened 30 July 2026. Tap a step.

The call offers up to €10 billion of public funding, from the EU and member states, and expects at least €20 billion of private investment, for up to seven sites in two lots. The InvestAI plan announced in 2025 had spoken of four to five gigafactories. Bids close on 12 November 2026 and selection is expected in early 2027, so no site has been chosen yet. Europe's model is closer to a public research facility than to Stargate: shared capacity for European labs, universities and companies.

VerdictSovereign AI factories are real, but slower and smaller than their announcements, and less sovereign than their name: almost all depend on US chips, US models and US licences. Their genuine advantages are land, energy and state capital. In the Gulf, a new risk has arrived that no company-built site in this series faced. The final part puts all nine case studies side by side to ask which bets are winning.

10. Reading the numbers

Stargate UAE
1 GW cluster within a 5 GW campus; first 200 MW due 2026 (G42), targeted Q3 then Q4 (trackers citing Mubadala and Khazna); not documented as running by 18 Oct 2026.
Humain
Up to 84 MW and ~27,000 NVIDIA GPUs in two phases (14 MW B300 from Q4 2026; 70 MW Vera Rubin from June 2027), 50 MW for a US client; goals of ~3 GW by 2030 and >6 GW by 2034. Earlier Riyadh/Dammam sites with 18,000 chips not confirmed operating ⚠️.
EU
Up to 7 gigafactories; €10B public, ≥€20B private; bids close 12 Nov 2026; 18 member states, 76 consortia interested (EuroHPC, Euronews).
Norway
230 MW + 290 MW potential; 100,000 GPU aim; Microsoft took capacity after OpenAI did not close its offtake (Quartz, TIME).
India
38,231 GPUs onboarded and 190 projects approved (government, Mar 2026); ₹10,372 crore five-year outlay; subsidised rates around ₹65–67 per GPU-hour (reported).
Security ⚠️
1 Mar 2026 strikes on AWS facilities (reported by DCD and others); UAE campus redesign (Reuters exclusive via secondary reports).
